segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Clinical questions, or it's a gray area, so I can have some… Kind of quick additional information. That I want to, of course, verify before maybe then asking a partner about it, that sort of thing.
segments.rationale: The participant describes using AI for uncertain clinical questions as a fast first pass, but explicitly says the output still needs verification before consulting a colleague.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It's been helpful. I've even used it… this clip, and look for this language, and look in the operative note, and did they say this? ... Figuring out ways to troubleshoot.
segments.rationale: The excerpt emphasizes that the tool was helpful for working through a documentation problem by suggesting what language and notes to inspect.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I didn't like, like, some long list of citations at the end. I didn't like citations as, yeah, like, numbers. I want to kind of know where it's coming from up front.
segments.rationale: The participant rejects long end-of-report reference lists and numeric citation styles, and asks for source provenance to be visible earlier.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Like, some of them, I think, said, like. PubMed... you got a little idea of where it was coming from. ... the sources appeared to actually go to the right spot, because… I think that's not always the case with ChatGPT.
segments.rationale: Trust increases when the participant can see recognizable source origins and when links match the claim, while prior source mismatches in ChatGPT reduce confidence.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I don't want it to be… you know, too long. I guess I'm not accustomed to looking at anything in a sort of, like, table format... I'm used to kind of a more chat GPT kind of conversational feel.
segments.rationale: The participant wants shorter outputs and states a preference for conversational prose over table-heavy formatting.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It wasn't too long, it was kind of to the point, it had a few citations, I could tell where they were coming from, they were legit... I don't have time to look through... like, too many, then I'm just overwhelmed.
segments.rationale: The participant identifies the preferred report as concise, credible, and manageable under time pressure, with excess references becoming overwhelming.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I liked when... It said the title of the, kind of, article or report it was... Cuz, if it was just a report. Anyway, I wanted to know, kind of, what I was getting myself into before I would click on it.
segments.rationale: The participant values seeing titles because they help judge whether a source is worth opening.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I would want... a summary... some evidence, but not so extensive... I think about a page is good. ... it would be... a nice way to have that incorporated in there, too... this is also an expert opinion.
segments.rationale: The participant specifies a target length, asks for some but not excessive evidence, and proposes adding expert opinion alongside the evidence summary.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I was just, like, trying to get them to help me figure it out... they said, go look in these spots... look in the operative report... And so, anyway, it just... like, I don't need evidence for that, right?
segments.rationale: The participant distinguishes a troubleshooting use case from literature review, saying this kind of operational reasoning does not require formal evidence display.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It was more of just helping me think through... Kind of a complex multi-step situation. Help me just troubleshoot it. ... not necessarily they didn't take the clip out. We need to look at other places.
segments.rationale: The participant values the tool because it helped reason through multiple steps and avoided a premature conclusion.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It could be embarrassing for them... and then embarrassing for me... I would have hated if I had, like, reached out to a surgeon... Sometimes I'm like, gosh, should I word this less stupid so I'm not embarrassed?
segments.rationale: The participant uses the tool partly to avoid embarrassment in interpersonal workflows, but also worries about whether someone might later read the query.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Shorter is good. I think one integrated into, like, an EMR is... would be nice for... like, HIPAA purposes... Easy integration, like, you don't even have to do any sort of, here's this info.
segments.rationale: The participant asks for shorter outputs and direct EMR integration to reduce manual data transfer and better fit privacy-sensitive clinical work.

analytic_memos.summary: This participant sees AI as useful primarily because it can provide quick orientation and help troubleshoot messy problems without the social cost of immediately asking a colleague. The participant does not want long, heavily referenced outputs; brevity is treated as essential for real clinical use. Trust is strongly tied to whether sources are visibly named, legible, and actually match the underlying claim. The participant prefers a conversational style over tables and wants to see article titles before deciding whether to click. For literature-like reports, the ideal output is about a page with a summary and a limited amount of evidence. The participant also imagines added value from integrating expert opinion rather than relying on citations alone. At the same time, the participant describes another class of use case—stepwise troubleshooting—where operational guidance matters more than formal evidence display. Integration into the EMR is framed as both a workflow convenience and a privacy-sensitive design improvement.
tensions_or_tradeoffs: Wants evidence and credibility, but only in a limited amount that does not create overload.
Values AI as a private space to ask basic questions, but also worries about whether someone might read the query later.
Sees literature-summary and troubleshooting tasks as both important, but not well served by a single report style.
